paras: The attempted lynching of William Patterson and Albert Turner was the siege of the Jefferson County jail in Louisville, Kentucky, by a mob intent on lynching the two Black prisoners, who were accused of fatally beating a domestic servant named Jennie Bowman. According to the wire account, the State militia guarded the jail for three days until the crowd dispersed, and both men were later hanged by law. The siege is known only from background paragraphs in reports of Patterson's execution on June 22, 1888, which in most versions date it to April 27, 1887; a Louisville dispatch that June also described a plot by a few citizens to lynch Patterson if he were pardoned.

Jennie Bowman worked as a domestic for a family in a "fashionable suburb" of Louisville and was beaten in the house about ten o'clock in the morning while the family was away; she later died of her injuries. Turner and Patterson, both described as "colored," were arrested on suspicion. Turner confessed at once and implicated Patterson, who denied any part in the crime.

Four days after the crime, on April 27, a mob surrounded the jail "bent on lynching the two negroes." The State militia was called out and guarded the prisoners for three days, keeping the mob at bay until "the excitement subsided" and the crowd dispersed. The reports give no size for the mob, name none of its members, and describe no shots, injuries or arrests.

Turner pleaded guilty and was hanged on July 1, 1887, declaring on the scaffold that Patterson was innocent. Patterson was tried and convicted, and the state's highest court affirmed the sentence. In February 1888 John Crow, a fellow prisoner, claimed that Patterson had confessed to him the Bowman murder and three others, a story Patterson denied.

A petition for pardon led Governor Buckner to respite Patterson for a month and then until June 22, after which he announced he would not interfere again. On June 17 a Louisville dispatch reported that "less than a dozen prominent citizens" had planned, if Patterson were pardoned, to go to the jail one or two at a time, seize the keys and hang him before the authorities could act. The group had met to make arrangements after the first respite, until "cooler heads" persuaded them that the governor would not intervene. Patterson was hanged in the jail yard on June 22, 1888, still protesting his innocence; the noose slipped and he strangled slowly, crying out four minutes after the drop. No report of arrests or prosecutions over the 1887 mob or the 1888 plot appears in the coverage.

The siege reached print only as a single background paragraph in the execution story, which ran on June 22 and 23, 1888, in the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer, the Washington Critic and the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer. Headlines centered on the hanging itself: "PATTERSON STRANGLED" in Wheeling, "Jennie Bowman Avenged" in Washington, "A Scaffold Horror" in Richmond and "The Murderer of Jennie Bowman Explates His Crime" in Memphis. The Richmond Dispatch's shorter version of the dispatch dropped the mob paragraph, and the New York Evening World omitted the mob entirely, dwelling instead on Patterson's scaffold speech.

Much of the coverage stressed doubts about Patterson's guilt, with the Wheeling report noting that "many people believe firmly in his innocence" and the Evening World calling his speech "the most vigorous protest of innocence possibly ever heard" from a condemned man. The Wilmington Daily Republican printed the pardon plot under the headline "On the Verge of a Lynching," calling it "a strange story" and passing no judgment on the plotters.

The versions disagree on the year: the Wheeling report dates the crime April 23, 1888 and the siege "April 27th," while the Critic and Lancaster version gives April 23 and April 27, 1887. The 1887 dating fits the rest of the coverage, which shows Patterson already condemned and respited by February 1888 and places the crime "last year." The Evening World alone dated the murder to June 21 of the previous year, said Bowman died defending the house from robbery, and had Turner hanged a month after the crime.
